Visual references (Lucas sent eleven images as mood references; they are described here in words. Some are film stills or photos of real people: they set a look and a tone only, and no character is based on anyone's face.)

**01 · Bar, close two-shot** (`01-bar-close-two-shot.jpg`). A dim, crowded dive bar at night.
Two people pressed close in the foreground: she faces camera-left with a wary look; he stands
right behind her, chin near her shoulder, looking past her. Their faces are lit low and warm
from the side, skin with a soft sheen, and everything else sinks into brown-black. Behind them:
amber wall sconces, a red neon strip, a cold green glow from a drinks fridge, small red points
of light along the bar, all soft in shallow focus. Intimacy that reads as threat.

**02 · Candlelit bar counter** (`02-candlelit-bar-counter.jpg`). A cramped bar lit by vintage
lamps: a green glass lantern, a red fringed shade, candles in glasses on the counter among the
bottles, a chalkboard menu behind. Heavy red and green colour, black corners, film grain and a
vignette, like an old snapshot. A couple sits close at the end of the bar, her in a white top,
him leaning in.

**03 · Record bar** (`03-record-bar.jpg`). A listening bar: a floor-to-ceiling wall of vinyl
records behind the bar, warm dome pendant lamps hung low, rows of bottles, backlit hi-fi
units. Patrons in silhouette; a man and a woman seated side by side at the bar, seen from
behind. Warm amber, mostly shadow.

**04 · Doubled portrait** (`04-doubled-portrait.jpg`). A pale woman with long auburn hair
stares into the lens, flat and cold, against black; a blurred second copy of her turns away
beside her, like a double exposure. A self split in two.

**05 · Bathtub, black and white** (`05-bathtub-bw.jpg`). A black-and-white photo in a tiled
bathroom. A young woman in a polka-dot blouse, an apron and rubber gloves holds up the head of
a charred, blood-slick body slumped in the tub, and smiles at the camera as if posing for a
family snapshot. Domestic calm and neatness right next to horror: she is pleasant, the scene
is monstrous.

**06 · The morning after** (`06-morning-after.jpg`). A warm, yellow-tinged snapshot taken from
the pillows, like a phone photo with the flash on. A man with long locs and a tattooed arm sleeps
face-down into the pillow, mouth open; the woman beside him is awake, a hand pressed to her
forehead, staring off, bored and uneasy. Soft focus, crumpled patterned bedding. He is out cold;
she is somewhere else in her head.

**07 · The abandoned hotel inside** (`07-abandoned-hotel-interior.jpg`). Inside an old,
abandoned hotel: a carved-leg pool table in the middle of a bare plank floor, a tall rack of
cues, a wood stove, a long table with spindle chairs, pressed-tin walls, an open white door.
Low sun slants through tall windows and throws lace-like patterns of light across the wall and
floor; everything else is dust-brown shadow, sepia and still, untouched for decades.

**08 · The desert motel** (`08-desert-motel.jpg`). An abandoned roadside motel in flat desert:
a big peeling "MOTEL" sign on steel legs with a red "OFFICE" arrow, a gutted two-storey block, a
long carport, palm trees and dry scrub in front, a pale washed-out sky, dusty faded-film colour.

**09 · The joy ride** (`09-joy-ride.jpg`). A vintage silver open two-seater convertible, 1950s
shape, seen from behind on a winding mountain road at sunset above a sea of cloud; the low sun
flares from the left, the light gold and warm; two people in the seats. The romantic, free
version of the drive, which the cold open plays against.

**10 · Two faces, sepia** (`10-two-faces-sepia.jpg`). A sepia portrait: a woman's composed face
in front, three-quarter to camera, chin resting on her hand, calm and pleasant. Behind her, a
second version of her face, half in shadow, stares straight into the lens with dark streaks
running down from the eye like black tears. The monster behind the composure.

**11 · The open road** (`11-open-road.jpg`). An aerial of a red vintage open-top sports car,
alone on a straight two-lane road through golden grassland at sunset. Hazy, warm, low light;
the grass moves in the wind; hills far off in the haze. Wide, lonely and golden.

brief.name: Limerence
brief.brand: None. This is an unbranded original drama; LIMERENCE is the project name.
brief.product_or_subject: Venus, a vigilante who falls into limerence with the unpunished men she hunts. The pilot covers her night with St. Jean and the road trip after it.
brief.one_line_brief: A vigilante who falls in love with every unpunished man she sentences drives her latest across the desert, laughing and filming him, still waiting for the dead man to love her back.
brief.objective: Route: commission (A07). A drama development exec who watches V01 and reads D01 asks for the pilot script or books a meeting. The signal is a script request or a meeting on the calendar.
brief.audience: Drama development execs at streamers and networks who are choosing which genre pilot to take to script. The eventual viewer is someone who follows true-crime cases online and has watched one close with nobody charged.
brief.key_message: Venus can punish any man the system lost, but her 'strong desire for reciprocation' is the one thing she can't satisfy: no man she hunts ever loves her back.
tone: Tender: play the cold open as a love story. Her laugh, her phone and her hands fixing his collar carry it. Jean's face is held back until his open eyes land, the one face shot the performance earns (taste note: hands before faces).
Genuine: play the bar banter as a real flirt and cut on the laughs, so the audience wants the straw house to stand even while it loses straws.
Clean: in the white apartment the horror is how tidy it is. Show a few dried drops, never a spray, and hold on the spotless room longer than is comfortable, like ref 05's calm next to horror.

Music: original. Venus puts on a trance-soul track in the white apartment to quiet herself, so the music is heard inside the scene (A08). Everywhere else the scene carries its own sound: tires, wind, straws on wood, a glass set down (taste note: sound design before music).
Not a glossy femme-fatale or gender-swapped Dexter: no voiceover explaining her code, no slow-motion hair, sex or blood, no gore.
verified_product_facts: Limerence is infatuation marked by a desire for the feelings to be returned, not mainly for sex.
The walls where she lives are covered in photos of the man, and none show the two of them together.
The bar game is called decorum; its goal is to see whether the house they build would last.
She carries a gun in her back pocket at the motel.
The man's name is St. Jean, called J.
Venus lures the men and kills them over a date.
The colour theme is white.
The man is dressed in all black, as her black hole.
Her meds are in her bathroom.
She hasn't taken the meds in weeks.
There is a small amount of dried blood behind the toilet seat in her apartment.
Trance-soul music plays to quiet her from feeling crazy.

deliverables.label: Pilot outline · the whole ~30-min episode (A01) for the commission pitch · Venus plays decorum with a man she has already sentenced, and the episode ends with the first photo of them together · unbranded · Season question (A17): the one man who tells the truth at decorum and seems to love her back, and whether she can sentence him

Cold open · pitch hero sequence and the pilot's first scene · Venus laughs and films a sleeping man across the desert until his open eyes show he is dead, then unpacks under a wall of his photos, none of them together · unbranded; LIMERENCE title card on the final frame only · no spoken lines (A15)

Teaser · 9:16 social and pitch-deck embed, rebuilt from V01 footage · her phone keeps recording a man who never wakes, and his eyes show why · unbranded; LIMERENCE card in the last 2 s; reads with sound off
Key art · pitch-deck cover and poster · Venus laughing at the wheel, Jean pale and still beside her in golden light · LIMERENCE title only
World frame · pitch-deck page · the motel wall of Jean photos, none of them together, groceries set out below · no text
Social frame · teaser post · a straw house on the bar between two glasses, one straw being pulled away · no text

must_include: The laughing joy ride, with Venus filming an unresponsive Jean, and then his pale, lost eyes
The pistol in her back pocket at the abandoned desert motel, which she checks is untouched before she unloads
The motel room she has kept (A14): walls of Jean photos, none of them together, and food and supplies set on the table
Decorum at the bar: straws won and lost, with Lucas's dialogue ('have we met before', the Naked and Famous, 'who slayed you my friend')
The all-white apartment with Jean in all black; the dried blood he wipes away and the red drops on the floor, both the previous man's (A13)
Her meds, untaken for weeks, and the trance-soul track she plays to quiet herself
The metal tin, slid over closed and opened only after Jean's line about love (A18)
The morning after (ref 06): Venus lies awake beside Jean, waiting for him to turn over, then remakes the white bed
The ending: the first photograph of them together (A06)
must_avoid: A voiceover explaining Venus's code, the drift toward Dexter (taste note: restraint over explanation)
Treating her meds as the explanation for the killings: they are seen, never named as the reason
Gore or blood spray in the white apartment: dried drops only
Slow motion to glamorise the drive, the sex or the death (taste notes)
Explicit nudity or sex in V01, V02 or the stills, because the pitch pieces have to be able to circulate
Any lost case based on a real, recognisable crime or victim; every case is fictional
Any character modelled on a face from Lucas's reference images; the references set look and tone only
Showing how the tin's contents are prepared or dosed; the method stays off screen
Real brands on screen (the Uber, the Raptors shirt) unless cleared; clearance is pending with the producer (A10)
The phrase 'female Dexter' in any public-facing material; it is an internal comparison only
brief.logline: A vigilante who falls in love with every unpunished man she sentences drives her latest across the desert, laughing and filming him, still waiting for the dead man to love her back.
brief.premise: Laughing, Venus drives through an empty desert town, filming the man asleep beside her, until his pale, open eyes show he is dead. At an abandoned motel, pistol in her back pocket, she unloads the luggage into the room she has kept for weeks: walls of Jean photos, none of them together. Flashback: a Thursday dive bar, Jean three nights drunk over a breakup, a stranger asking "have we met before?" She has watched him for months; his ex's domestic-violence report went nowhere. Her game, decorum, is her verdict: each lie costs him a straw. In her all-white apartment Jean wipes dried blood off the toilet; her meds sit untaken; a trance-soul track quiets her. She slides over her metal tin and asks for one true thing about love, his last straw; he gives her a line, and she opens it. By morning the "trip" has stopped his heart; she lies awake beside him, waiting for him to turn over, then remakes the white bed until it is spotless. At the motel she seats Jean at the table, takes the first photograph of them together, and pins it beside the first photos of the next man.

story_seed.protagonist: Venus, a vigilante who falls into limerence with every unpunished man she sentences
story_seed.want: for Jean to love her back and tell her one true thing, so the house they build could last
story_seed.obstacle: Jean is the man she has been hunting, and each lie he tells at decorum costs him a straw
story_seed.turn: in her all-white apartment she slides over her metal tin and asks for one true thing about love, his last straw; he gives her a line, she opens the tin, and by morning the 'trip' has stopped his heart
story_seed.ending: At the motel she seats Jean at the table, takes the first photograph of them together, and pins it beside the first photos of the next man.

from the side, skin with a soft sheen, and everything else sinks into brown-black. Behind them:
amber wall sconces, a red neon strip, a cold green glow from a drinks fridge, small red points
of light along the bar, all soft in shallow focus. Intimacy that reads as threat.

**02 · Candlelit bar counter** (`02-candlelit-bar-counter.jpg`). A cramped bar lit by vintage
lamps: a green glass lantern, a red fringed shade, candles in glasses on the counter among the
bottles, a chalkboard menu behind. Heavy red and green colour, black corners, film grain and a
vignette, like an old snapshot. A couple sits close at the end of the bar, her in a white top,
him leaning in.

**03 · Record bar** (`03-record-bar.jpg`). A listening bar: a floor-to-ceiling wall of vinyl
records behind the bar, warm dome pendant lamps hung low, rows of bottles, backlit hi-fi
units. Patrons in silhouette; a man and a woman seated side by side at the bar, seen from
behind. Warm amber, mostly shadow.

**04 · Doubled portrait** (`04-doubled-portrait.jpg`). A pale woman with long auburn hair
stares into the lens, flat and cold, against black; a blurred second copy of her turns away
beside her, like a double exposure. A self split in two.

**05 · Bathtub, black and white** (`05-bathtub-bw.jpg`). A black-and-white photo in a tiled
bathroom. A young woman in a polka-dot blouse, an apron and rubber gloves holds up the head of
a charred, blood-slick body slumped in the tub, and smiles at the camera as if posing for a
family snapshot. Domestic calm and neatness right next to horror: she is pleasant, the scene
is monstrous.

**06 · The morning after** (`06-morning-after.jpg`). A warm, yellow-tinged snapshot taken from
the pillows, like a phone photo with the flash on. A man with long locs and a tattooed arm sleeps
face-down into the pillow, mouth open; the woman beside him is awake, a hand pressed to her
forehead, staring off, bored and uneasy. Soft focus, crumpled patterned bedding. He is out cold;
she is somewhere else in her head.

**07 · The abandoned hotel inside** (`07-abandoned-hotel-interior.jpg`). Inside an old,
abandoned hotel: a carved-leg pool table in the middle of a bare plank floor, a tall rack of
cues, a wood stove, a long table with spindle chairs, pressed-tin walls, an open white door.
Low sun slants through tall windows and throws lace-like patterns of light across the wall and
floor; everything else is dust-brown shadow, sepia and still, untouched for decades.

**08 · The desert motel** (`08-desert-motel.jpg`). An abandoned roadside motel in flat desert:
a big peeling "MOTEL" sign on steel legs with a red "OFFICE" arrow, a gutted two-storey block, a
long carport, palm trees and dry scrub in front, a pale washed-out sky, dusty faded-film colour.

**09 · The joy ride** (`09-joy-ride.jpg`). A vintage silver open two-seater convertible, 1950s
shape, seen from behind on a winding mountain road at sunset above a sea of cloud; the low sun
flares from the left, the light gold and warm; two people in the seats. The romantic, free
version of the drive, which the cold open plays against.

**10 · Two faces, sepia** (`10-two-faces-sepia.jpg`). A sepia portrait: a woman's composed face
in front, three-quarter to camera, chin resting on her hand, calm and pleasant. Behind her, a
second version of her face, half in shadow, stares straight into the lens with dark streaks
running down from the eye like black tears. The monster behind the composure.

**11 · The open road** (`11-open-road.jpg`). An aerial of a red vintage open-top sports car,
alone on a straight two-lane road through golden grassland at sunset. Hazy, warm, low light;
the grass moves in the wind; hills far off in the haze. Wide, lonely and golden.

content.logline: A vigilante who falls in love with every unpunished man she sentences drives her latest across the desert, laughing and filming him, still waiting for the dead man to love her back.
content.format_rationale: Series pilot. Lucas's hint names it, and his own engine repeats. Venus 'finds male killers, rapist, and DV and sex offers whose case get lost' and 'lures them and kills them over a date', so every episode brings a new man, a new game of decorum and a new wall. Across the season the stakes rise toward the one man who tells the truth at decorum and seems to love her back, and whether she can sentence him (A17). Runner-up: short film, which has one woman, one want and one cost. It lost because a short has to end the engine that the idea wants repeated. Build: D01 outlines the whole pilot. V01 is the cold open, the strongest self-contained sequence. It has no spoken lines, only her laughter, and its hook plays on its own.
content.premise: Laughing, Venus drives through an empty desert town, filming the man asleep beside her, until his pale, open eyes show he is dead. At an abandoned motel, pistol in her back pocket, she unloads the luggage into the room she has kept for weeks: walls of Jean photos, none of them together. Flashback: a Thursday dive bar, Jean three nights drunk over a breakup, a stranger asking "have we met before?" She has watched him for months; his ex's domestic-violence report went nowhere. Her game, decorum, is her verdict: each lie costs him a straw. In her all-white apartment Jean wipes dried blood off the toilet; her meds sit untaken; a trance-soul track quiets her. She slides over her metal tin and asks for one true thing about love, his last straw; he gives her a line, and she opens it. By morning the "trip" has stopped his heart; she lies awake beside him, waiting for him to turn over, then remakes the white bed until it is spotless. At the motel she seats Jean at the table, takes the first photograph of them together, and pins it beside the first photos of the next man.
what_makes_it_specific: Kept: Lucas's cold open as he wrote it. The laughing joy ride with a man who seems asleep, the reveal of his pale, lost eyes, the pistol, the motel she keeps, and the wall of photos 'yet none of them together'.

Kept: the decorum straw game and its dialogue, the names Venus and St. Jean ('J'), the all-white apartment with Jean in black as her black hole, the dried blood he wipes away, the untaken meds, the aftermath of the night, and the female-Dexter engine of luring unpunished men over a date.
Obvious version: a gender-swapped Dexter. A cool, in-control vigilante seduces a predator, the last scene reveals she is the killer, and a voiceover lays out her code.

Differs by what it costs her: Venus is not in control. She is in limerence with every man she condemns, and killing him is the only way he can never leave her. The pilot opens after the kill, so the suspense is why she still loves him, not whether she will do it. The cost shows on screen: the tin stays closed until his line about love, because she was hoping he would pass (A18).
Added detail (A04): decorum is her private verdict. She already knows the true answers, and each lie Jean tells takes a straw off the house. His line about love costs him the last straw.
Added ending (A06): the first photograph of the two of them together, pinned beside the next man's photos. It pays off Lucas's 'none of them together' and shows the series engine in one frame.
Added payoff: Venus's 'let's take a trip' comes true twice, first as the tin and then as the road trip with his body.
Added season question (A17): the one man who passes decorum. The pilot's pattern of one lie, one straw and one sentence exists so that a later episode can break it.
Product role: none. This is an unbranded original drama with nothing to sell, so there is no product to become decoration.

Taste notes: every one is followed and none is broken. Following 'Hands before faces', Jean's face is held back until the dead-eyes reveal. Following 'Sound design before music', the only music plays inside the scene. Following 'Restraint over explanation', her meds are seen but never named as the reason. 'The product is a tool, then a hero' does not apply because there is no product.
content.brand: None. This is an unbranded original drama; LIMERENCE is the project name.
content.product_or_subject: Venus, a vigilante who falls into limerence with the unpunished men she hunts. The pilot covers her night with St. Jean and the road trip after it.
content.objective: Route: commission (A07). A drama development exec who watches V01 and reads D01 asks for the pilot script or books a meeting. The signal is a script request or a meeting on the calendar.
content.audience: Drama development execs at streamers and networks who are choosing which genre pilot to take to script. The eventual viewer is someone who follows true-crime cases online and has watched one close with nobody charged.
content.key_message: Venus can punish any man the system lost, but her 'strong desire for reciprocation' is the one thing she can't satisfy: no man she hunts ever loves her back.
tone: Tender: play the cold open as a love story. Her laugh, her phone and her hands fixing his collar carry it. Jean's face is held back until his open eyes land, the one face shot the performance earns (taste note: hands before faces).
Genuine: play the bar banter as a real flirt and cut on the laughs, so the audience wants the straw house to stand even while it loses straws.
Clean: in the white apartment the horror is how tidy it is. Show a few dried drops, never a spray, and hold on the spotless room longer than is comfortable, like ref 05's calm next to horror.

Music: original. Venus puts on a trance-soul track in the white apartment to quiet herself, so the music is heard inside the scene (A08). Everywhere else the scene carries its own sound: tires, wind, straws on wood, a glass set down (taste note: sound design before music).
Not a glossy femme-fatale or gender-swapped Dexter: no voiceover explaining her code, no slow-motion hair, sex or blood, no gore.

evidence.specificity: All six previous notes were addressed, and the next department can act on the page. The turn is now an action in order: "She slides over her metal tin and asks for one true thing about love, his last straw; he gives her a line, and she opens it." The build is counted: "V01 needs 3 locations (desert road and town, motel exterior, motel room), 2 on-camera roles and 2 consistent characters, 1 voice (her laughter, no words), an estimated 15–20 generated shots, 3 hand shots (phone, pistol, groceries)." Sound is named: "tires, wind, straws on wood, a glass set down." It stops short of 9 because the ending's "first photos of the next man" is not placed anywhere in V01. That wall is in the same motel room on the same day, so design cannot tell whether a second face is already on the wall in the hero sequence.
evidence.distinctiveness: The swap test fails for any other vigilante story. "By morning the 'trip' has stopped his heart; she lies awake beside him, waiting for him to turn over, then remakes the white bed until it is spotless." "At the motel she seats Jean at the table, takes the first photograph of them together, and pins it beside the first photos of the next man." That ending pays off Lucas's own "none of them together" and shows the series engine in a single frame. The difference from the rival pitch is what it costs her, not the tone: "Venus is not in control. She is in limerence with every man she condemns, and killing him is the only way he can never leave her." The rewritten logline now names the title concept instead of the meds: "still waiting for the dead man to love her back."
evidence.fit: Lucas can find his idea at every point. His cold open, the decorum dialogue, the all-white room, Jean in black, the dried blood, the untaken meds, trance/soul and the female-Dexter engine are all in must_include. The aftermath he asked for is now built on ref 06: "she lies awake beside him, waiting for him to turn over." The meds are "seen, never named as the reason", and the logline no longer opens with "Off her meds." Every verified fact carries an exact quote from the idea. Two small drifts remain in the fact paraphrases. "The walls where she lives" contradicts A14 ("the motel is where she builds his wall") and the premise's "the room she has kept for weeks". "Trance-soul music plays" states A08's reading of "Trans/soul" as though it were verified.
evidence.craft: Every previous craft note landed. The premise is 195 words and ends on its ending, and story_seed.ending matches it word for word. The tin order holds across the premise, story_seed.turn and A18. A09 is split into A09 (route), A15 (counts) and A16 ("a 5 s shot in a moving convertible in which a still, open-eyed passenger holds consistency"). The dialogue claims agree: "0 spoken or lip-synced lines." A10 names its owner: "Owner: the producer. Status: pending, nothing cleared." Video totals 105 s (90 + 15) against the 120 s limit. One continuity break remains in the core mechanism. The D01 label says "Venus plays decorum with a man she has already sentenced", but A18 says "opening it is her sentence, so she was hoping he would pass." The label also sits against the premise's "Her game, decorum, is her verdict." A commissioner reading the outline label would get the opposite of the brief's central idea.

Clean: in the white apartment the horror is how tidy it is. Show a few dried drops, never a spray, and hold on the spotless room longer than is comfortable, like ref 05's calm next to horror.

Music: original. Venus puts on a trance-soul track in the white apartment to quiet herself, so the music is heard inside the scene (A08). Everywhere else the scene carries its own sound: tires, wind, straws on wood, a glass set down (taste note: sound design before music).
Not a glossy femme-fatale or gender-swapped Dexter: no voiceover explaining her code, no slow-motion hair, sex or blood, no gore.
verified_product_facts: Limerence is infatuation marked by a desire for the feelings to be returned, not mainly for sex.
The walls where she lives are covered in photos of the man, and none show the two of them together.
The bar game is called decorum; its goal is to see whether the house they build would last.
She carries a gun in her back pocket at the motel.
The man's name is St. Jean, called J.
Venus lures the men and kills them over a date.
The colour theme is white.
The man is dressed in all black, as her black hole.
Her meds are in her bathroom.
She hasn't taken the meds in weeks.
There is a small amount of dried blood behind the toilet seat in her apartment.
Trance-soul music plays to quiet her from feeling crazy.

normalized_brief.logline: A vigilante who falls in love with every unpunished man she sentences drives her latest across the desert, laughing and filming him, still waiting for the dead man to love her back.
normalized_brief.premise: Laughing, Venus drives through an empty desert town, filming the man asleep beside her, until his pale, open eyes show he is dead. At an abandoned motel, pistol in her back pocket, she unloads the luggage into the room she has kept for weeks: walls of Jean photos, none of them together. Flashback: a Thursday dive bar, Jean three nights drunk over a breakup, a stranger asking "have we met before?" She has watched him for months; his ex's domestic-violence report went nowhere. Her game, decorum, is her verdict: each lie costs him a straw. In her all-white apartment Jean wipes dried blood off the toilet; her meds sit untaken; a trance-soul track quiets her. She slides over her metal tin and asks for one true thing about love, his last straw; he gives her a line, and she opens it. By morning the "trip" has stopped his heart; she lies awake beside him, waiting for him to turn over, then remakes the white bed until it is spotless. At the motel she seats Jean at the table, takes the first photograph of them together, and pins it beside the first photos of the next man.

content.audience_tension:
Viewer (who the show is for): people who follow true-crime cases online, on the night a case they have followed for months closes with nobody charged and they keep reading anyway [brief.audience; the moment is H1]. In their voice: I want the man who walked to be punished, yet months later I still look him up, waiting for a confession he will never give me. [H1] The loss they'd hate to admit: the man they want punished now has more of their attention than the person he hurt, and wanting justice has turned into a one-sided attachment that no verdict would end. The referent is the man who walked, which makes the viewer a direct mirror of Venus: she falls for the man she sentences, carries out the sentence herself, and still waits for him to love her back. Take the show away and the tension still exists. Viewer proxy (assumption, used only if V02 or S03 go public): followers of true-crime podcasts, forums and creator channels. Rejected drafts: H7 (guilt at cheering for a killer) and H10 (attachment to the victim, not to him).

Buyer (who acts): drama development execs at streamers and networks, at the point where they sort genre pitches into the few they take to script [brief.audience]. Proxy (assumption): a named list the producer or agent emails a private screener link to. There is no media buy. Execs buy when they believe this viewer exists. Their own conflict, a hook this audience already binges against the fear of buying a copy, is the Barrier and not the tension [H2, H8].
content.desired_behavior:
Goal: a paid script commission or development deal for Lucas's pilot, the step before a series order. For the buyer, return becomes revenue if the repeating engine ('every episode brings a new man, a new game of decorum and a new wall' [F19, content only]) brings viewers back episode after episode [H9]. Release cadence is the buyer's call (see assumptions).
From: the exec reads the logline and files LIMERENCE with the other vigilante pitches [H2].
To: after watching V01 and reading D01, the exec requests the pilot script or books a meeting with Lucas [brief.objective].
Jobs:
V01 (16:9, 90 s, private screener link, laptop, sound on assumed): makes the exec feel the love story before the eyes land, so they open D01.
D01 (outline, read after V01): the exec decides here. It proves the episode's shape, that the engine repeats [F19], and the season question [F20].
V02 (9:16, 15 s, deck embed and forwardable link, must read muted): gets the colleague it is forwarded to to open V01.
S01 (2:3, deck cover): the proposition in one frame, with her laughing and him still.
S02 (16:9, deck page): shows the world's rule, his wall with no photo of them together [F2].
S03 (4:5, in-feed muted, posted only if the producer releases social): a reminder of decorum. It is not expected to produce a request.
content.product_relevance: Moment: between pitches, an exec opens the producer's screener link and watches V01. Without a want of its own, the piece gets filed with the comps as a gender-swapped vigilante [H2]. What fixes it: [F1] 'a desire for the feelings to be returned, not mainly for sex' turns her motive from control into longing, and [F2] 'none show the two of them together' shows that longing in one frame. Scene that must land: the V01 drive. Venus laughs and films a man who never wakes until his open eyes show why. The feeling it leaves is tenderness that carries on after the dread begins. D01 lands it again at the end [F17]: the first photo of them together, pinned beside the next man. For the season: because punishing can't make a man love her back, the season asks what she does with the one man who seems to, and whether she can sentence him [F20, A17]. That carries the proposition past the pilot into D01, where the exec decides. For the viewer, it speaks to the night a case they followed closes with nobody charged and the man who walked still has their attention [H1]. Barrier: fatigue with vigilante-killer shows and the reading of this one as a copy [H2, H8], plus a creator with no checkable track record supplied. Permission: not established. No credits, attached producer or prior work were supplied (see blocker).
content.single_minded_proposition: Punishing the man the system lost can't make him love her back.

hypotheses: H2 Riskiest: V01's reveal moves execs from reading LIMERENCE as a gender-swapped vigilante copy to reading it as a show about her wanting him to love her back. It goes first because if it dies, the script request fails. If H1 dies, the proposition still stands on H7 or H10. Test: send the logline alone to 5 development readers, then V01. Each time, ask unprompted what it reminds them of and what it is about. Owner: producer. Kills it if: after V01, fewer than 3 of 5 say it is about her wanting him to love her back rather than about a vigilante code.

H1: when a case closes with nobody charged, people who follow it online keep watching the man who walked and wait on him for something he will never give (a confession, an apology, a sign). The attachment is to him, which mirrors Venus directly. Test: six short calls with people who followed a case that closed with no charge. Ask how it felt when it closed and what they still do about it. Keep it unprompted: do not name or ask about the man, and do not use the words love or attachment. No case detail from these calls enters the show. Owner: producer. Kills it if: fewer than 3 of 6 describe, unprompted, still looking up the man who walked or waiting on him for something. If they describe waiting on the victim, the family or the case instead, revive H10. If they describe only justice and guilt, revive H7.

H3: no series on air or announced leads with the clause only LIMERENCE owns: she falls in love with every man she sentences, and the sentence is how she keeps him. The nearest threats are listed from common knowledge, unverified and for internal use only. You and Killing Eve both lead with a killer's obsessive, unreturned love. In Promising Young Woman the heroine falls for a man who turns out to be implicated in the case she is avenging. Dexter leads with the code. Test: the producer checks the clause against You, Killing Eve and Promising Young Woman first, then scans current and announced slates and loglines. Owner: producer. Kills it if: any of them, or any series on air or announced, has a lead who falls for each person she punishes and uses the punishment to keep him.

H4: V01 works as the hook only if the tenderness holds after the eyes land, with her still laughing. Test: show a rough cut to 5 cold viewers and ask what they felt just before and just after the eyes. Owner: editor. Kills it if: most felt dread before the eyes (the reveal is telegraphed) or felt nothing tender (the love story did not play).

H5: an exec's script request depends more on the D01 pages showing the engine repeat and escalate [F19, F20] than on the pilot story alone. Test: ask the 5 development readers from H2 which D01 page would decide a script request. Owner: Lucas. Kills it if: fewer than 3 of 5 point to the engine or season pages. If they point to Venus's want instead, D01 leads with her want.

H6: the untaken meds, seen and never named, read as texture and not as the cause of the killings. Test: one sensitivity read of D01 by a reader with lived or clinical mental-health experience. Owner: producer. Kills it if: the reader takes the meds as the reason she kills.

H9: viewers come back from episode to episode for the repeating engine (the next man, the next round of decorum, the next wall), and that return is how the series earns for the buyer. Test: after V01 and a one-page D01 summary, ask 5 viewers from the true-crime proxy, unprompted, what they would want to see next. Owner: producer. Kills it if: fewer than 3 of 5 name something the engine repeats, such as the next man, the next round of decorum or whether she falls again. If they name only who Jean was, D01 has to bring the next man in earlier.

H7 Rejected: In their voice: I want the man who walked to pay, yet I feel guilty cheering for a killer. Every vigilante series already owns this moral-dilemma tension, so it fails the competitor-name test. Revive if: the H1 calls surface justice and guilt but never attachment.

H8 Rejected (exec tension): In their voice: I need a hook this true-crime audience already binges, yet I'd hate to be the one who bought the gender-swapped copy. It describes the buying decision, not what the show speaks to, so it is kept as the Barrier. Revive if: H2 shows execs never get past the copy question. The pitch then states the difference before the feeling.

H10 Rejected: In their voice: I grieved for someone I never met, yet nobody who knew them knows I exist. Here the attachment is to the victim. It mirrors Venus less directly, because she falls for the man and not for the person he hurt. Revive if: the H1 calls describe waiting on the victim, the family or the case rather than on the man who walked.

assumptions: Market and language: English-language drama for North American streamers and networks. This is inferred from the North American brands in Lucas's idea and is not confirmed.

Client and money: there is no brand. The client is Lucas as creator, and LIMERENCE is the working title (development's working brand). The revenue path is a paid script commission or development deal, then a series order. Subscriber value downstream belongs to the buyer.
Release cadence (weekly, or all episodes at once) is the buyer's call. H9 tests return from episode to episode, not a weekly schedule.
Reach: V01 and D01 go privately from the producer or agent to a named list of execs, with no media buy. V02 and S03 go public only if the producer decides a public teaser helps the pitch.
Viewing conditions: V01 is watched on a laptop with sound on. V02 must read muted. S03 is muted in-feed.

Evidence: Lucas's raw idea text, including 'whose case get lost', is not used as evidence. F13 (the logline) carries 'the man the system lost' as content. Because the old F15 was dropped, the former F16-F19 are now F15-F18, and the ending proof point is now F17. F19 and F20 quote development's format_rationale and the D01 label as content only, as the reviewer directed.
Proposition contingent on: A02 (Jean's ex's domestic-violence report went nowhere) for 'the man the system lost' in the pilot. F13 supports it for the series as a whole.
Proposition contingent on: A18 (the tin stays closed until his line about love). It shows she hoped he would pass, which keeps her love real rather than a trap.

Proof points are held to four. F2 is not a standalone proof point: F17's ending pays F2 off and carries 'can't make him', while F2 still does work in product_relevance, S02 and the competitor fallback. F18 restates F1's support in story terms. F3, F5, F14-F16, F19 and F20 are story mechanics or season content rather than proof of the proposition.
Proof points leave out F4 and F7-F12 (gun, colour, meds, blood, music). They are execution, or they argue a second idea (her instability), and under must_avoid the meds must never read as the reason.
Sample sizes are consistent: 5 development readers for H2, H5 and success criterion 4, 6 viewer calls for H1, and 5 cold viewers for H4 and H9.
Comparable titles in H3 are common knowledge, unverified and internal only. The phrase 'female Dexter' stays out of all public-facing material.
Success thresholds are studio go/no-go lines, not market benchmarks. No statistic is claimed anywhere.

Taste notes, which the file flags as example notes and not Lucas's own: the proposition follows 'Restraint over explanation' (it names her want, never her code) and 'Dry over sentimental', and breaks none. 'The product is a tool, then a hero' does not apply because there is no product.

blockers.issue: Alternative: key_message ('Venus can punish any man the system lost, but her strong desire for reciprocation is the one thing she can't satisfy: no man she hunts ever loves her back.') is not carried as the proposition. The main reason: 'no man she hunts ever loves her back' contradicts A17, the season question D01 must carry (the one man who tells the truth at decorum and seems to love her back). It is also a 29-word line with two beats, and 'any man' and 'the one thing' are not supported by any fact. Proposed instead: 'Punishing the man the system lost can't make him love her back.' This leaves the season question open.
blockers.resolution: Approve the 12-word proposition, or keep key_message as pitch copy with 'any', 'the one thing' and 'ever' removed so it no longer rules out A17.

blockers.issue: The competitor check (H3) has not been run. No one has checked the clause only LIMERENCE owns (she falls for every man she sentences, and the sentence is how she keeps him) against the nearest threats, You, Killing Eve and Promising Young Woman, or against current and announced slates. The comps stay internal.
blockers.resolution: Before the first send, check those three titles first, then scan current and announced slates and loglines. If one matches, sharpen the proposition to the wall with no photo of them together (F2).

evidence.specificity: The creative director could build routes from this page without asking a follow-up question. The viewer tension names a behavior, a moment and a referent: "on the night a case they have followed for months closes with nobody charged and they keep reading anyway" and "In their voice: I want the man who walked to be punished, yet months later I still look him up, waiting for a confession he will never give me. [H1]". Every deliverable gets a job with its placement and sound, for example "V02 (9:16, 15 s, deck embed and forwardable link, must read muted): gets the colleague it is forwarded to to open V01". The To is measured as a rate with the counting rule stated: "execs who request the pilot script or book a meeting, per 10 execs sent V01 and D01. An exec who does both counts once." Prior note 2 is fixed: the referent is now "the man who walked", the 'answer me' echo is gone, and the viewer block comes before the buyer block. It gets 9 rather than 10 because one job, V02, has no measure (see notes).

routes.central_idea: She can take his life, but she can't make his hand close on hers.
routes.emotional_promise: The ache of watching her squeeze his hand and wait, still smiling, for a squeeze that never comes back.
routes.product_role: SAFE. No product (unbranded drama); the subject is Venus, played as a lover on a date. Job in frame: her hand asks for a response he can't give (the squeeze, the collar, the arm across his chest), which is the reciprocation limerence wants. First appearance: her hand in his at 0 s. Her face comes at 32 s and Jean's at 40 s (hands before faces). Brand assets: LIMERENCE title card on V01's final frame only and in V02's last 2 s. No logos: the car, phone, groceries and clothes are unbranded (A10). Proof: 'Limerence is infatuation marked by a desire for the feelings to be returned, not mainly for sex.' 'She carries a gun in her back pocket at the motel.' 'The walls where she lives are covered in photos of the man, and none show the two of them together.' 'The man is dressed in all black, as her black hole.'
routes.visual_language: Palette: #F2EEE6 her white shirt; #111111 Jean's black shirt; #C9A45C dry gold grass at the roadside; #A9ADA6 the silver body of the open two-seater (A11); #B5452E the motel's red OFFICE arrow. Light: hard low sun from the driver's side raking across both seats, then flat dusk; in the motel room, last sun through gaps in boarded windows striping the wall. Framing: close and still at shoulder height across the two seats, hands first; Jean's head turned to the door, sunglasses on, until 40 s; one wide from the roadside when the dust devil crosses. Texture: road dust on the dash and on his black sleeves, sun-cracked seat leather, fine grain. Sound: tires on grit, wind over the open car, her laugh, the phone's shutter. No score (taste note: sound design before music). The title card lands in silence.

Look: close and still across the seats, hands first; hard low sun raking both seats; dust on black cloth; tires and wind, no score.

5-14 s [G]: an empty desert town slides past behind him (shuttered pumps, one dead traffic light swinging). She straightens his collar; his head rests on the door, turned away, sunglasses on.
14-24 s [G+C]: over her shoulder, her phone records him 'asleep' in gold light, head toward the door; the shutter clicks; her laugh shakes the picture (C: generic REC dot, no brand UI).
24-32 s [G]: a dust devil crosses the road ahead. She brakes, laughing, and throws her arm across his chest the way you'd catch a passenger; his weight tips into her arm and stays there. She eases him back against the seat and drives on.
32-40 s [G, recurring face; fallback G profile only]: her face for the first time, laughing at the wheel, eyes on him.
40-48 s [G, first try in the moving car (A16); fallback G, parked at the motel]: a bump; his sunglasses slip; his eyes are open, pale and dusted, and don't blink in the wind. The one face shot.

routes.central_idea: She isn't collecting trophies; she's trying to get into one photograph with him.
routes.emotional_promise: The pang of her thumb resting on the flip-camera icon over his open eyes, then sliding back: not yet, not like this.
routes.product_role: STRETCH. No product; the subject is Venus as the photographer who is never in the frame. Job in frame: her phone, a lover's camera she won't turn on herself. The flip-camera icon she touches and leaves shows the want: before the eyes (18-26 s) it plays as shyness; after them (50-56 s), as 'not like this, not yet'. The wall repeats it without her. The pilot pays it off when the first photo of them together, at the table, is her first use of the front camera (A06). First appearance: the phone's upright frame at 0 s. Her face at 34 s, when she lowers the phone; Jean's at 42 s. Brand assets: LIMERENCE title card on V01's final frame only and in V02's last 2 s. The phone UI (REC dot, running timer, flip-camera icon) is an original design with no OS or maker's marks; owner: production design; clearance pending with the producer under A10, not claimed as cleared. No other logos. Proof: 'The walls where she lives are covered in photos of the man, and none show the two of them together.' 'Limerence is infatuation marked by a desire for the feelings to be returned, not mainly for sex.' 'She carries a gun in her back pocket at the motel.' 'The man is dressed in all black, as her black hole.'
routes.visual_language: Rule: while she films, the picture is her phone's screen, a narrow upright frame centred in black with a red REC dot, a running timer and a flip-camera icon (original UI). When she lowers the phone, the frame opens to full width: the world as it is. Palette: #D7261E the REC dot; #111111 Jean's black shirt; #F2EEE6 her white shirt; #C9A45C gold dust on the dash; #3E5670 blue dusk over the road. Light: inside the phone, low gold sun behind her flaring on the lens, sinking to dusk over about an hour of timer; at dusk the phone's own video light, small and hard, on the dust of his black collar. Outside the phone, flat blue dusk. In the motel, one battery lantern on the table. Framing: handheld at arm's length inside the phone, jolting when she laughs, with his head turned to the door, cheek on the headrest, so only collar, jaw and one arm of the sunglasses show until 42 s; outside the phone, locked off and still. Texture: inside the phone, compression, wind clipping the mic, a fingerprint smear on the lens; outside it, clean and quiet. Sound: the phone's mic, with wind roar and her laugh loud and close. When the frame widens, the wind drops to tires and engine heard from outside the car. No score; the title card lands in silence.

routes.central_idea: Decorum isn't her trap; every straw is a chance she's praying he'll take.
routes.emotional_promise: The held breath as her fingertip rests on the last straw still standing, hoping he'll save their house.
routes.product_role: BRAVE. No product; the subject is Venus as a judge who wants to acquit. Job in frame: the straws, decorum's clock. The cold open braids a silent bar night into the drive; each straw she draws out at the bar cuts to the car. The braid stops with one straw still standing: her fingertip rests on it, and we hard cut to his open eyes. The last straw is his line about love in the white apartment (F16, A18), which D01 plays; V01 shows neither the tin nor the verdict causing the death. First appearance: straws at 0 s, the drive at 4 s, her face at 58 s. Brand assets: LIMERENCE title card on V01's final frame only and in V02's last 2 s. No bar, drink or car logos (A10). Proof: 'The bar game is called decorum; its goal is to see whether the house they build would last.' 'Limerence is infatuation marked by a desire for the feelings to be returned, not mainly for sex.' 'She carries a gun in her back pocket at the motel.' 'The walls where she lives are covered in photos of the man, and none show the two of them together.' That each lie costs a straw is premise content resting on A04, not a verified fact.
routes.visual_language: Palette: #B8322A a red fringed lampshade over the bar; #2F6B4F the drinks fridge's green glow; #D9C08A the bar straws; #111111 Jean's black shirt; #C9A45C gold desert grass. Framing: close and still on hands at counter height in the bar and at the same height across the car seats, so every hard cut matches hand to hand; Jean's head turned to the door until 54 s. Texture: in the bar, film grain, a vignette and sticky dark wood; in the desert, dust on black cloth. Sound: straws laid on wood, a glass set down, ice, and a murmured room with laughter but no words (A15). In the desert, wind and tires. Each straw drawn out is a cut. No score.

content.recommendation_rationale:
Proposition: 'Punishing the man the system lost can't make him love her back.' Proof beat, 50-56 s: after his open eyes the phone comes back up, REC 01:04:55, her thumb rests on the flip-camera icon, then slides back; the lens stays on him. 18-26 s plants the same pause before the eyes, so after them it reads as 'not like this, not yet'. Success: at least 3 of 5 development readers say unprompted, after the 90 s V01, that it's about her wanting him to love her back; V02's post-eyes flip beat (11-13 s) serves the 4-of-5 muted read.
Gives up: the objective camera for most of the drive, Venus's face until 34 s, Jean's until 42 s, and full screen width for 40 of 90 s (0-34 s and 50-56 s).
Failure: at 18-26 s and 50-56 s the thumb on the icon is too small to read at phone size, and thumbs garble in generation. Fix: the C fallback keeps the choice: the screen flips to the front camera for under a second, catches both of them (his head slumped away at 18-26 s; his open eyes aimed past the lens at 50-56 s), then flips back to him. At 42-50 s (A16) the open eyes in a moving car may not hold; the fallback moves the reveal to the parked car at the motel.
Kill test: in the H2 test, fewer than 3 of 5 readers say after V01 that it's about her wanting him to love her back, and they read the phone as trophy-taking or as her keeping herself out of frame with a body. Then the photograph idea has failed, not the craft. Switch to R1, whose unreturned squeeze carries the want with no camera.
Case R1: tone ('Tender... Her laugh, her phone and her hands fixing his collar carry it') and the V01 label as written. Pick R1 if Lucas wants the drive in the objective camera with her face in the first act, or if the phone frame tests as a gimmick.
Case R3: the D01 label's season question (A17, the one man who tells the truth at decorum), read with H5. Pick R3 if readers say the engine pages (F19: new man, new decorum, new wall) decide a script request, because only R3 puts decorum in the cold open. Lucas must also accept V01 spending the bar flashback.

assumptions: The three most familiar openings in this genre (internal, no titles named): (1) a vigilante killer's cold open with a voiceover laying out the code; (2) the femme-fatale seduction with slow-motion glamour and a last-scene reveal that she is the killer; (3) a true-crime pastiche with case-file cards, news audio and 'unsolved' titles. All three routes avoid 1 and 3. R1 subverts 2: her touch asks rather than controls. R2 subverts the killer's trophy photo. R3 subverts 2 by making the seduction game a chance rather than a trap.

Ten one-liners were drafted; the three kept differ in reframe, device and structure. R1: linear, objective camera, the hand as device; its idea costs 'a killer's touch is control'. R2: told through her phone's frame, widening at the reveal, the front camera as device; it costs 'the photos are trophies'. R3: two braided timelines, omniscient POV, the straws as device; it costs 'the seduction game is a trap'. [changed] R1's previous idea ('The kill is already over; the only suspense left is whether he'll love her back') restated the development premise, so every route's example served it. It failed the pairing test and was replaced. Other cut drafts: 'the sentence is the first day he can't walk out' (reads as control, against F1) and 'a dead man can't lie at decorum'.
There is no product. product_role describes the job of the device that carries the proposition and Venus's role in frame. The taste note 'the product is a tool, then a hero' does not apply.

All beats are tagged G or C: V01, V02 and the stills are generated end to end (A09), no shoot budget is authorised and no renders were supplied, so no beat is tagged P or R. Every reveal beat depends on the A16 test shot.

Creative additions not found in Lucas's idea or the facts, for Lucas to approve: the dead traffic light, the dust devil with her arm catching his weight, and the unreturned squeeze (R1); the stop sign nobody else will reach, the REC timer, the flip-camera icon, the under-a-second front-camera flip, the phone's video light, turning his chin with two fingers, and the battery lantern (R2); the bent straw in his pocket and the wind lifting it (R3); the oranges (all routes).

[changed] R2, question for Lucas: it changes his cold open's camera. 40 of 90 s are seen inside her phone's upright frame (0-34 s and 50-56 s); her face is withheld until 34 s and Jean's until 42 s; the pilot's ending (A06) becomes her first use of the front camera for a photograph. The fallback's under-a-second flip is a live preview, not a photograph, so A06's 'first photograph of them together' still stands. No beat is dropped.
